Cold Water Swimming boom

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
There has been a global resurgence of cold water or “wild” swimming as people find ways to combat and protect themselves from the impacts of Covid-19. The social and health benefits of cold water swimming have been extolled for decades, a tradition dating back centuries. The ladies private pool on Hampstead Health in the heart of London dates back to the 1930 when the women extolled the benefits of a dip in 1.5 degrees for a quick immersion, turning prawn pink in a matter of minutes.
And it’s not only those crazy old ladies in Camps Bay there is the Hot Chocolate club that meets every Sunday morning for a swim and then Hot Chocolate afterwards to warm up. The exhilaration of the shared experience of the icy water fuels the connections as they hang out at a local coffee bar to warm up. For many isolated people it’s broken down barriers and they connect with people they would never have encountered.


Summary:
It’s an age-old tradition but those groups have tended to be pockets of one or two people. But since the virus struck the numbers have surged of both young and old, taking to the icy water off Camps Bay and Clifton and right down to Simon’s Town
During the week they meet at dawn, that’s 7am in midwinter you will find the Camps Bay tidal pool full of people who called the “ bobbers” rather disparagingly by the long distance sea swimmers. They just want to immerse themselves in cold water, followers of the Wim Hoff method of deep breathing and cold water immersion which has a host of perported physical and psychological benefits.
Swimming to Robben Island used to make the front page of the newspapers, now 30 people are doing the Robben Island swim a month, from the most unlikely people who are really scared of the waves to Tri athletes like Ryan Stramrood who has swum it 116 times, he uses it as a training swim for his more extreme ice swims, because its so challenging.


Further information:
There is a lot written about how it enhances circulation, supercharges the metabolism, boosts the immune system and creates an endorphin high. Some attest to feeling less pain from chronic conditions, as cold water increases blood flow, improving circulation and allowing inflammation to heal more quickly. The immune system is ramped up because cold water helps boost the white cell count when the body is forced to react to changing conditions and becomes better at mobilising its defences. Cortisol, a stress hormone, is released from your adrenal glands, which maintains this state for minutes to hours, while a surge of beta-endorphin hormones in the brain provides pain relief and gives a sense of euphoria.
The endorphin high is created because cold water brings us close to the pain threshold and endorphins are released when we are in pain to help us cope. Stress is reduced, the boredom cycle is broken and a sense of calm and wellbeing prevails. It’s also said to help people cope better with other stressors in their life as their brain trains to deal with the extreme shock of the cold water. It stimulates the Vagus nervous system, the opposite of the fight and flight mechanism in our bodies which COVID has exhausted. People suffering from crippling inflammatory disease like Crones disease, arthritis, and even anxiety and depression find significant relief from their symptoms with regular cold-water swimming. It’s long been documented that athletes take ice baths after extreme training to reduce swelling and inflammation, physiotherapist apply ice packs to injuries as it causes the blood vessels to constrict reducing blood flow to the area.
There is a whole “science” behind how to handle the body’s shock reaction and acclimatisation to cold water to avoid drowning and heart attacks. People can drown within minutes when plunged into extreme icy seas as they involuntary gasp and suck in icy water. The body’s core temperature plummets and they become hypothermic. It’s critical that people warm their core temperature afterwards to stop it from continuing to drop so the ritual of warm clothes and flasks of hot beverage and beanies is all part of the culture. There are those who stay in for long swims and take it very seriously, slowly increasing their endurance, and then there are others who rush in and immerse themselves for as long as they can bear the shock, building up their pain threshold.
Wild and cold-water swimming is allowing people to reconnect with themselves and nature in a time of extreme stress, safely outside gyms and clubs. A safe place for young and old no matter what their co-morbidities. There is a lovely cross section of characters who are bursting to share their passion.

Script: Taking to the icy waters is a growing international trend under Covid 19. The benefits of cold water have been extolled since 400 BC as a natural antidepressant, metabolism, and immune booster. This group is here at dawn all year round, first oxygenating their blood by deep breathing, before they take to the icy waters for 20 minutes. Known as the bobbers, because they just hang out in the cold water

Link : It could be the loneliness of lockdown, the plunging economy, or the search for health and longevity but there are groups like this meeting at dawn from Camps Bay to Simons Town, and extolling the virtues of cold water swimming

Script: At 83 Helen Boonzier never misses a morning
Helen “It makes me feel so wonderful all day
Script. And leader of the group Vaughan Pierce, keeps raising the bar
Vaughn. “I put in a rule that we are going to swim everyday during winter and every day everyone has arrived its all about community, it's all about us coming together this has saved me personally during lockdown
Script: And everyone has their own buzz, from keeping fit to those who have just learnt the joy of swimming. Julia Hamel took the plunge for the first time in her 40’s with the help of her good friend Karien Cherry
Julia: I started this two years ago, I turned 45 and I was like, you know, my life's not really passing me by but I've had a bucket list of things that I want to do

Derek: But you could have done it in a warm swimming pool, not out here in the ocean.

Julia: Go, big or go home Derek, why would I want to go into a bath? I could go in a bath at home.

Script: Watching Julia master swimming, inspired others to step into the water, she’s ended up teaching them and now- they’re all hooked.

Julia: That's been amazing. I've met a whole lot of people that actually I probably wouldn't have actually met otherwise.

Karien “ I always say it shocks the bullshit out of you are just so present in that moment, it’s a real mental emotional high

Script: That’s the endorphins kicking in, - and as their tolerance for the cold-water builds- their heart rate drops, giving the same sense of calm as meditation
Justin: I was staring at another year of Lockdown and scratching my head as to what to do to get out of my own funk,
Script: Justin Nurse couldn’t afford the gym into the 2nd year of lockdown
Justine “I just met my sister here at Silvermine for a swim, we swam two lengths and said, let's meet in a few days’ time. We did that. And then we said, what about Robben Island? And then after we'd conquered our first hour of cold water at Clifton, it became a real possibility
Script: Justin and his sister reflect a trend of ordinary people setting their sights on what used to only be tackled by top athletes like Lewis Pugh. Now 16-year-olds like Kelsey Chiang have swum Robben Island, and they say it’s all thanks to one man, Derrick Frazer - he gave up his life as an accountant to piloting open ocean events. He has personally shepherded just under 1000 Robben Island crossings
Frazer: I've taken the fastest swimmer, the record breaker cross, and that was just a whirlwind. I've taken some of the slower swimmers, but to see the average swimmer and get across on their first Robben Island crossing is just absolutely special.

Link: A Robben Island swim used to make the front page of the newspapers, now there are 50 people a month making the 7. 4 half km swim, at temperatures as low as 12 degrees centigrade - there is no such thing as an easy Robben Island swim

Derrick “ If you swim a Robben Island and you've got a kilometre to go and you get out I'll push them through and talk them through it. One of our sayings is that we make dreams happen.

Script: When Maura Sanderoff heard her friend had swum the island, Derek helped her achieve her dream
Maura “You see someone that you think is kind of your same level of swimming, strength. And that's what switched it on for me, but now I have to try this That swim is iconic, you know, for anyone to do.

Script: Losing a leg to osteosarcoma at 16, the sea had always been her happy place. She has swum the island 4 times now, once to raise money for her prosthetic leg
Derek: Maura go back and describe that very first, Robben Island, swim

Maura: It's a surreal feeling Derek . It's it it's hard to describe the excitement, the nerves, the intrepidation , you know, are you safe in the water? And I've got a husband who's beyond anxious.

Landing on Blouberg Beach and your family all there to welcome you that's the best part,so I swam with a whole lot of wonderful people, and that camaraderie is wonderful

Script: Everyone has their demons to fight, and Justin is no stranger to life’s curveballs, losing his 2 year old daughter in a tragic accident

Justin. Halfway through the Robben Island swim, there's just this infinity of blue water around you, it kind of brings home that my own insignificance or how small I am really in comparison to everything else

Derrick . Robben Island is a lot tougher than a well known race like the comrades I think. And the fantastic thing with cold water swimming is the fastest swimmers really appreciate the slower swimmers, a lot more than you would get in any other sport, because they know that they in the water twice as long, suffering twice as long.

Script: Like paraplegic Pieter Du Preez who was told it was impossible, and was one of Derek’s toughest crossings, but he did it and survived.

There is a great deal of scientific research extolling the benefits of coldwater swimming, from boosting the cardiovascular system to improving insulin tolerance. People also claim it helps manage their anxiety and depression, explains nutrigenetist and open ocean swimmer Yael Joffe

Derek: Yael what’s the biggest take away of braving the icy waters?

Yael: This concept of stress resilience, that when we go into the cold water and over time, learn both physically and mentally how to manage the cold, our mental and physical ability to manage stress has been improved and that is .the key, that we build stress resilience in the ocean, that we apply to all the other stresses in our life.

Script: But it’s all about gradually building that mental and physical tolerance

Yael: One of the great concerns I have is that everyone's kind of discovered cold water swimming and it's become super popular and almost cultish I would say when actually it's an extreme sport.

Script: Hypothermia is the real danger which ever swimmer has encountered at some point, even the most experienced

Yael: The difference between feeling cold in the water and having hypothermia is very difficult to differentiate because you're always cold. So, I have this thing where I count and when I can when I can't count to 20, I know that I'm starting to lose cognitive ability

Script: And once they out, the warmup ritual is critical to stop their core temperature dropping any further

Link: And if the icy ocean isn’t enough, a 10 minute ice bath is the next level, these days they used by top athletes internationally but what are the dangers and benefits for the rest of us?

Sean: Just jumping in can get cardiac arrhythmias, which is why I'm here to look after them. And that's probably the biggest danger, hypothermia, clearly, if you're in the water for long enough.

Script: But cold-water specialist Dr Sean Gottschalk was keeping a watchful eye over the Bobbers

Ice baths are rapidly becoming the next big thing, and people keep setting their sights on longer ocean swims. 8 km around Cape Point, then there is the equivalent of the English Channel, 33 km across False Bay.

Mastering one’s own body and mind by inviting the cold in, one stroke at a time, seems like the sanest response - to such unpredictable times.

And I've got a husband who's beyond anxious

21 Seconds” From hanging out in the icy water tidal pools in mid-winter, to long open ocean swims - there a growing trend in Cape Town of taking to the ocean “You get completely shocked out of anything else that is in your mind and you are just so present in that moment, it’s a real mental emotional high”

Tues PROMO T 170 : Taking to the icy waters is a growing trend over the last year under Covid. The benefits of cold water swimming have been extolled since 400 BC it’s claimed to be a natural antidepressant, immune-booster and metabolism reviver by some, but for many it’s just a way of overcoming the loneliness of lockdown.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: There has been a global resurgence of cold water or “wild” swimming as people find ways to combat and protect themselves from the impacts of Covid-19. The social and health benefits of cold water swimming have been extolled for decades, a tradition dating back centuries. The ladies private pool on Hampstead Health in the heart of London dates back to the 1930 when the women extolled the benefits of a dip in 1.5 degrees for a quick immersion, turning prawn pink in a matter of minutes. And it’s not only those crazy old ladies in Camps Bay there is the Hot Chocolate club that meets every Sunday morning for a swim and then Hot Chocolate afterwards to warm up. The exhilaration of the shared experience of the icy water fuels the connections as they hang out at a local coffee bar to warm up. For many isolated people it’s broken down barriers and they connect with people they would never have encountered.
metadata.Summary: It’s an age-old tradition but those groups have tended to be pockets of one or two people. But since the virus struck the numbers have surged of both young and old, taking to the icy water off Camps Bay and Clifton and right down to Simon’s Town During the week they meet at dawn, that’s 7am in midwinter you will find the Camps Bay tidal pool full of people who called the “ bobbers” rather disparagingly by the long distance sea swimmers. They just want to immerse themselves in cold water, followers of the Wim Hoff method of deep breathing and cold water immersion which has a host of perported physical and psychological benefits. Swimming to Robben Island used to make the front page of the newspapers, now 30 people are doing the Robben Island swim a month, from the most unlikely people who are really scared of the waves to Tri athletes like Ryan Stramrood who has swum it 116 times, he uses it as a training swim for his more extreme ice swims, because its so challenging.
metadata.Further information: There is a lot written about how it enhances circulation, supercharges the metabolism, boosts the immune system and creates an endorphin high. Some attest to feeling less pain from chronic conditions, as cold water increases blood flow, improving circulation and allowing inflammation to heal more quickly. The immune system is ramped up because cold water helps boost the white cell count when the body is forced to react to changing conditions and becomes better at mobilising its defences. Cortisol, a stress hormone, is released from your adrenal glands, which maintains this state for minutes to hours, while a surge of beta-endorphin hormones in the brain provides pain relief and gives a sense of euphoria. The endorphin high is created because cold water brings us close to the pain threshold and endorphins are released when we are in pain to help us cope. Stress is reduced, the boredom cycle is broken and a sense of calm and wellbeing prevails. It’s also said to help people cope better with other stressors in their life as their brain trains to deal with the extreme shock of the cold water. It stimulates the Vagus nervous system, the opposite of the fight and flight mechanism in our bodies which COVID has exhausted. People suffering from crippling inflammatory disease like Crones disease, arthritis, and even anxiety and depression find significant relief from their symptoms with regular cold-water swimming. It’s long been documented that athletes take ice baths after extreme training to reduce swelling and inflammation, physiotherapist apply ice packs to injuries as it causes the blood vessels to constrict reducing blood flow to the area. There is a whole “science” behind how to handle the body’s shock reaction and acclimatisation to cold water to avoid drowning and heart attacks. People can drown within minutes when plunged into extreme icy seas as they involuntary gasp and suck in icy water. The body’s core temperature plummets and they become hypothermic. It’s critical that people warm their core temperature afterwards to stop it from continuing to drop so the ritual of warm clothes and flasks of hot beverage and beanies is all part of the culture. There are those who stay in for long swims and take it very seriously, slowly increasing their endurance, and then there are others who rush in and immerse themselves for as long as they can bear the shock, building up their pain threshold. Wild and cold-water swimming is allowing people to reconnect with themselves and nature in a time of extreme stress, safely outside gyms and clubs. A safe place for young and old no matter what their co-morbidities. There is a lovely cross section of characters who are bursting to share their passion.
